questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am very fond of the French language and culture, which were two important factors for me. I wanted to study in a French speaking country to improve my language skills. This was the most important factor, since I knew that choosing a French bachelor probably would come with its difficulties, so the academic/career oportunities were not too important for me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The study program was very hard since it was in French but I loved living in Paris. So living in Paris made up for the tough study.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite difficult. Sorbonne Université, at least the science faculty, is very disorganized and there wasn't a lot of information about anything. If there is something that is not clear or information is missing you have to take contact to your coordinator at Sorbonne. I had a very nice coordinator who helped a lot with course registration and other practical things such as a new learning platform (Moodle) and mail, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
My coordinator at Sorbonne was a big help. She was helpful, but I had to reach out to her to get any information, so the information doesn't come by itself.
The best way to get in contact is definitely showing up at the office in person, since an email correspondance can take a few days.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There was little to no information about the program and the faculty so you had to find all the information yourself. Everyone is pretty kind and helpful when you ask them.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I lived in Fondation Danoise at Cité Universitaire. It was a great place to live! There are other danish people but also international students from other houses in Cité. 
I also applied for housing through the Sorbonne application and was granted a CROUS (French collegium).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you live inside of Paris it does not matter where you live. It is easy to get to campus since there are many busses, metro and train everywhere. But it is nicer to live closer to campus, so I could recommend finding something on Rive gauche (the south side of the Seine).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think students are satisfied with CROUS which are usually pretty cheap I think, but I really enjoyed staying in Cité Universitaire. I know some who found a place on different housing websites as well and stayed in a studio or coloc.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registration was not bad, you get all information on your KUmail and then you just have to fill out all information.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You had to fill out different information about yourself, uploading passport, picture for a student card, etc.  You could also sign up for housing. It was pretty straightforward as I remember it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
My Erasmus-coordinator was helpful if information was missing or something wasn't clear. He could take a few days to respond, and in the middle of registration he went on vacation for 2 weeks. 
But, it will all work out, they seem to be very large and understanding if anything goes wrong.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
This was the most difficult process. First of all, I had to learn the course codes and I ended up registering for courses on the 6th semester instead of the 5th semester the first time (L3 is year 3 and the number after 'SV' (5) is the semester - at least on the bachelor). There were multiple classes I wanted to take, but the bachelor has a very strict structure so it is not easy to compose your own schedule. I had to follow the obligatory courses like the rest of the students, since these are on monday-tuesday-wednesday (UE tronc-commun) and then all the optional courses (UE complémentaire) were thursday-friday.
I had by accident chosen an UE complémentaire that hadn't been accepted as a limited-optional (begrænset-valgfri) course at KU and had to change it to another course the week before courses started. It was luckily possible to change, just show up at the coordinators office.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Ask your coordinator for the course schedules to see what time and days the different courses are. There are many courses that overlap and it does not say anything about it in the course catalogue. So to figure out what courses are actually available and possible to take, the course schedule is the most important thing. Look at the proposed schedule on the Sorbonne website for your study. This helps to see what options there are.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
There are no English bachelors at Sorbonne, and no courses taught in English on the 5th semester, so everything was in French. This made it much harder to focus and understand what was going on in the beginning of the semester. As I learned the vocabulary and got better at French, it became easier to manage, but still harder than if it had been in English. 
I was allowed to write my exams in English, I just had to ask the professors about it. This was such a help since I would've stressed more if I had to write in French.  

There are no books for the courses, so everything the professors say and what is shown on the slides are on the exams. I think it is more important to show up to the different lectures and classes to understand the context since not all the important information is written on the slides. 

There is a google drive for the students, made by the students, with notes for lectures and old exams. This became the most important tool for me during the semester. There are also whatsapp groups for all courses where all information and questions are sent. None of these are provided by the administration or professors, only the students. I found out from other international students and by asking the French students about it.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I don't think the level of the courses were more difficult than they would have been at KU, but since it was in French it was way harder.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It is very different to KU. There are no books, the days are much longer because there are more classes and lectures in a day to make up for the lack of books and self-study. The lectures (CM) and TD's are each 2 hours without a break and most days were from 8:30h to 18h. There are many midterms, papers and presentations to do during the semester. 

I took 7 courses, compared to max. 2 at a time at KU (block structure), which made the work load a bit overwhelming at times. The amount of ECTS for most courses are 3 or 6. The workload of the 3 ECTS courses are, in my opinion, way to big for the amount of credits given.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
LU3SV515 - Neurophysiologie et Physiologie des grandes fonctions 
LU3SV517 - Biologie du développement des Plantes
LU3SV518 - Microbiologie
LU3SV524 - Les microorganismes pathogènes 
LU3SV541 - Cerveau et comportement
LU3FLE01 - French course FLE (science faculty)
SIAL-FLE - online french grammar course from faculté des Lettres

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I recommend all of them. They are all very interesting and I don't think it is something we are taught at KU. There are more teaching in specific diseases, bacteria, functions which can be difficult to remember because the information is not that broad.
LU3SV515 is a pretty difficult course with an extremely large curriculum. 
LU3SV541 was very interesting with topics such as conscience, emotions, addiction and different experimental methods to study the brain.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I don't think there were any unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The monthly transport pass (navigo) was more expensive than I imagined. Restaurants were a bit cheaper than Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not not sign up for anything at Sorbonne, but I know there are different sports and clubs. Some sports you can get ECTS for.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I don't know about cultural or social activities. There are many different sports like rock climbing, fenching, yoga and swimming.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Parismus events like walks around Paris, trips and parties.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are many things to see in Paris but also many cities/countries that are easy and close by (Luxembourg and Belgium). Museums are free for students under 26 years old. Train tickets from SNCF can be pretty cheap sometimes. Walking around in Paris is nice.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was easy. Paris is not so different from other european cities. Most things are in french and most people only speak french, even the students, but if you speak french it is not difficult to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I did not end up socializing with any of the french students, only the international students. The french students seem very closed off and didn't make an effort to speak to me just like I didn't try either. There is almost no group work and no one (not even the french students) talk to each other during class. L3 in biology is huge, with around 400 students, so there are no social events either inside the study.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The french students are not very likely to small talk, but I guess it is kind of the same in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The amount of museums and other cultural things around Paris. Parisians seem to go more out for dinner during the week, which is a nice way to make a weekday fun.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Better to speak french at a C1 level. I spoke B2 when I arrived, it was manageable but very hard. 
Show up to every class, it helps with exams and other information.
Trust that everything will fall into place. It is possible to change courses the week before the fall semester, the year structure is first out during the summer and I wasn't aware of the startday of any of my courses except for a few days before.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It is important to write formal emails and adress the professors as M. or Mme.
Definetly use the whatsapp groups and google drive for studying and reviewing.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting friends from all over the world and living in Paris.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Studying in french.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Even though the study was difficult, the experience of living in Paris and being abroad made up for it all.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
